say: This is not theory. Two real cases. In New York in 2023, two lawyers asked ChatGPT for past court decisions to support their client. It made the cases up, with quotes, and when the lawyer asked if they were real, it said yes. Nobody checked. The judge fined them and their firm 5,000 dollars, and made them write to every real judge whose name was on a fake decision. In Canada in 2024, Air Canada's chatbot invented a refund rule for a customer whose grandmother had died. The airline argued the chatbot should answer for what it said. The tribunal disagreed: the company is responsible, and the airline paid. So who paid for the mistake: the tool, or the people? (Expected: the people.) Exactly. The tool never signs. You do. (Optional, closer to our work: in 2025, Deloitte Australia refunded part of a government fee after a report with made-up references and a made-up court quote.)
